content.text:
**Recruiters generally scan for a match first, then read for evidence.** It’s less “Let me learn your whole story” and more “Does this person look relevant enough to interview?” The exact process varies, but initial scanning followed by closer evaluation is a common approach. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&hl=en&utm_source=openai))

### 1. First pass: “Is this plausibly a fit?”
They look for basic alignment:
- Relevant experience and skills.
- Required qualifications.
- Employment history that fits the role.

At this stage, the question is whether you meet the requirements—not whether every bullet is impressive. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Make your target role and strongest relevant experience easy to spot. Don’t make someone piece together your fit from scattered clues.

### 2. Closer read: “What have they actually done?”
If the initial fit is there, they examine your experience, skills, and qualifications more carefully before deciding whether to move you to a screening call or interview. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Write bullets that give evidence rather than just name responsibilities. For example, a hypothetical rewrite:

> **Vague:** “Responsible for customer onboarding.”  
> **Specific:** “Redesigned onboarding for 40 enterprise accounts, reducing average setup time from 12 days to 8.”

Use real numbers when available; otherwise describe scope, complexity, or a concrete outcome.

### 3. Decision: “Is there enough here to justify a conversation?”
Resume review is a screening step, not the final hiring decision. The immediate outcome may simply be an invitation to a phone screen. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Optimize for a clear, credible case—not a complete autobiography. Put the most relevant evidence first, explain unfamiliar job titles, and cut material that doesn’t help establish fit.

### What about the ATS?
Software may come before or alongside human review. Some systems extract titles, skills, dates, and experience; some employers enable AI-assisted matching. There isn’t one universal screening process across employers. ([support.greenhouse.io](https://support.greenhouse.io/hc/en-us/articles/41131616864283-Talent-Matching-Data-Processing-FAQ?utm_source=openai))

**A useful test:** Give someone your resume for a brief glance, then ask: “What role am I suited for, and what’s the strongest evidence?” If they can’t answer, make those two things more obvious.
